Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.activity_title: Unlocking Friendship: Words and First Impressions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.59): two words that come to mind about friendship.
Let us read (p.59): what do you call a friend in your own language?

homework.task_brief: Let us read (p.59–60): fill in the blanks — words meaning partner, buddies, companion, classmates.

time_bands.activity: Open discussion: ask students to share two words they associate with friendship, collecting responses on the board. Invite brief explanations for each word chosen.
Read aloud the opening pages of 'The Chair' (p.59–60) with students following in their textbooks. Pause at key moments to let students notice how Mario talks about his many friends.
Class discussion on the multilingual dimension: students share what they call a friend in their home languages. Build a short board list of friendship words across languages, noticing similarities.
Brief closing reflection: ask students whether having many companions is the same as having many friends. Collect two or three responses and leave the question open for the story to answer.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the story of Mario, a boastful boy who believes he has an enormous circle of friends; grounding students in the word 'friend' in multiple languages activates their prior knowledge and sharpens the distinction the story will develop. A common early pitfall is conflating 'companion' or 'classmate' with 'true friend' — the word-list discussion surfaces this confusion before reading deepens it. Students who have not completed the fill-in blanks task at home can attempt it independently using context clues from the page.

periods.activity_title: The Grandfather's Wager: Reading Part I

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61): True/False — Mario proud of many friends; what grandfather took from attic.

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the friendship word-list from the previous discussion, reminding students of the distinction between companion, partner, and true friend. Set a guided-reading purpose: watch how grandfather challenges Mario.
Read aloud p.60–61 with students tracking the text. Pause after the grandfather produces the invisible chair from the attic to ensure students picture the scene vividly.

Work through the 'Let us discuss' questions at p.61 as a whole class: judge the True/False statement about Mario's pride and discuss what grandfather brought from the attic. Invite students to share predictions about whether Mario will face challenges.
Quick pair-share: each student tells a partner one prediction about whether Mario's 'magic' will work, and why. Two pairs share aloud before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The pivot of the narrative is grandfather's wager — a fruit chaat bet that most of Mario's supposed friends are merely companions, not true friends. Students often miss that the invisible chair is a metaphor for the invisible tests that every friendship must pass; a brief teacher clarification after reading steadies this. The oral prediction task is kept quick and paired so all students, including hesitant speakers, have a chance to articulate their thinking.

periods.activity_title: Mario Falls — and Finds His Friends: Reading Part II

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.64): True/False first attempt; fill blank — bet was about; match characters to actions.
Let us discuss (p.64): describe the chair in two words; why was it tricky to sit on.

time_bands.activity: Shared reading of p.61–64: teacher and students take turns reading paragraphs aloud, covering Mario's repeated falls and the moment Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently hold him up. Encourage expressive reading at the key scene.

Work through the 'Let us discuss' questions at p.64 as a class: judge the True/False about Mario's first attempt, fill in the blank about the bet, and complete the character-action matching task orally before students record answers.

Discuss the two extract questions: what two words describe the chair, and why was it tricky to sit on. Students share responses in pairs, then a few answers are shared aloud to consolidate understanding of the chair as both object and metaphor.

periods.teacher_notes: The climactic scene — three friends silently moving to support Mario while the rest laugh — carries the story's moral weight. Students may reduce this to 'the three friends were nice'; push them toward the idea that true friends act without being asked. Ensure students distinguish the chair's physical trickiness (it is invisible and has no visible support) from its metaphorical function as a test of genuine care.

periods.activity_title: What the Chair Reveals: Close Reading and Reflection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.64–65): why grandfather called chair 'special'; why Mario says technical problem.
Answer questions (p.65): what was the bet; what happened first time Mario sat; how he found real friends.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud p.64–65 at a measured pace, focusing on the exchange between Mario and his grandfather after the school test and the explanation of what the chair's magic actually revealed.

Discuss the extract questions: why grandfather called the chair 'special', and what Mario meant by a 'technical problem' when he kept falling. Encourage students to look at the exact words in the text before offering interpretations.
Students answer the three factual questions at p.65 in writing: what was the bet, what happened the first time Mario sat, and how he identified his real friends. Share and correct answers as a class.
Quick whole-class discussion: do students think the invisible-chair test is a fair or unfair way to find true friends? Collect two contrasting views to honour different readings of the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The section on why grandfather called the chair 'special' requires students to hold the chair's literal and metaphorical meanings simultaneously; scaffold this by asking what the chair reveals rather than what it does. The question about Mario's 'technical problem' is a humour marker in the text — help students see Mario's embarrassment and dignity together. The three factual questions require students to read carefully and distinguish between the bet's terms and the bet's outcome.

periods.activity_title: Friends for Life: Extended Responses and Personal Reflection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Answer questions (p.65): personal meaning of 'friends for life'; other ways to identify real friends.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the closing paragraphs of the story (p.65), where all four children visit grandfather, eat fruit chaat, and decide to use the invisible-chair test for life. Allow the fable's tone to settle before moving to the reflective questions.

Students write an extended response to the question 'What does "friends for life" mean to you?' drawing on the story's events and their own understanding. Circulate and prompt students who are stuck to think of a moment from the story first.

Students write a second extended response: what other way, besides the invisible-chair test, might help someone find real friends? Encourage them to draw on their own experience or on the story's logic.
Two or three students share their responses aloud. Briefly draw out any fresh ideas about friendship that go beyond the story's own answer, celebrating personal insight.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full arc — Mario's boast, grandfather's wager, the test at school, and the fruit-chaat celebration — students now have enough narrative context to write with depth. A common pitfall is students paraphrasing the story rather than offering their own viewpoint; prompt them by asking what they personally believe, not what Mario discovered. The extended response questions are the richer pair from the comprehension set and deserve unhurried writing time.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Manu: A Story of Support and Friendship

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.68): fill in five blanks while listening to Manu describe Monika's support.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening context: Manu is a new student at a school who found things very difficult — students predict in pairs what kind of support she might have needed, sharing one idea each.
Read the transcript aloud clearly and at moderate pace (p.73), with students listening and attempting to fill in the five blanks at p.68. Remind students to note key words as they hear them.
Read the transcript aloud a second time at the same pace. Students check and complete any blanks they missed on the first listening.

Whole-class check: go through each blank in order, inviting students to share answers and confirm against the transcript. Brief discussion: in what ways is Monika's friendship similar to what Guneet, Asma, and Deepa showed Mario in the story?

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript tells of Manu's experience as a new student guided by Monika — a real-world friendship that mirrors the narrative's theme of support in difficult moments. Students who mishear or miss a blank on the first listening should be reassured that the second reading will give them a second chance; this models careful listening rather than anxiety. The comparison with Guneet, Asma, and Deepa keeps the thematic thread alive without requiring any prior unit to have occurred.

periods.activity_title: Qualities of a True Friend: Paired Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.68): choose four friend qualities; give reasons using guided sentence starters.

time_bands.activity: Read the list of friendship qualities on the board (loving, honest, kind, caring, loyal, polite, respectful, team-worker, understanding) and the provided sentence starters aloud. Model one example: 'I feel my friend should be honest because truth builds trust.'

Students work in pairs: each person selects four qualities and uses the sentence starters to explain their choices to their partner. Encourage partners to ask a follow-up question after each quality is shared.
Groups of four (two pairs) compare their choices: which quality did everyone pick? Which was most surprising? Each group nominates one quality they all agreed on and one they debated.

Whole-class share-out: each group states their agreed quality and their debated quality. Teacher facilitates a brief discussion connecting the chosen qualities back to the characters of Guneet, Asma, and Deepa in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The sentence starters in the task are scaffolds that give hesitant speakers a structured entry into conversation; encourage all students to use them rather than treating them as optional. A common pitfall is students listing qualities without giving reasons — the follow-up-question instruction in pair work directly addresses this. Connecting student-chosen qualities to Guneet, Asma, and Deepa anchors the abstract discussion in concrete narrative examples without requiring any specific prior discussion to have taken place.
materials: Blackboard with qualities list and sentence starters

periods.activity_title: Writing to a Friend: Completing and Crafting Messages

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.69): choose correct words in brackets to complete Mario's message to Guneet.
Let us write (p.69): write your own message to your best friend.

time_bands.activity: Read the sample messages Mario writes to his friends on p.69, drawing students' attention to tone, word choice, and format. Discuss as a class what makes a message feel warm and personal.

Students individually complete Mario's message to Guneet by choosing the correct word in each bracket. Pairs then compare their choices and justify any differences, referring back to the story's events.

Students write their own message to their best friend, using ideas from the story and the qualities discussed in class. Encourage them to think of a specific moment or quality that matters to them personally.

Two or three students share their messages aloud. Acknowledge specific, concrete expressions of friendship in the messages, reinforcing the difference between generic praise and genuine, reasoned appreciation.

periods.teacher_notes: The guided task of completing Mario's message provides a bridge between reading for meaning and writing independently; students who struggle to start their own message can return to the sample messages on p.69 for structural and tonal cues. A common pitfall is vague statements like 'you are a good friend' — encourage students to name a quality and give a reason, echoing the speaking task's structure. Both writing tasks begin and conclude within this unit; no prior draft or previously produced material is required.

periods.activity_title: Root Words and Suffixes: Building Words from the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.65): divide friendly, suddenly, talking, carrying, called, showed into root word and suffix.
Let us learn (p.66): match root words to suffixes and write sentences using each formed word.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the concept of root words and suffixes using the example 'friend + ly = friendly' from p.65. Write the six story words on the board and ask students to try splitting each one before the table is introduced.
Students complete the table at p.65 dividing all six words into root word and suffix. Review answers as a class, noting spelling changes where they occur (e.g., carrying — carry + ing).

Students work through the root-word and suffix matching task at p.66 (magic, care, celebrate, laugh, wonder, help, friend, courage) with the given suffix set. For each formed word, students write one sentence of their own.
Pairs share one word-and-sentence combination each. Briefly draw attention to any spelling changes observed, consolidating the pattern without turning it into a spelling drill.

periods.teacher_notes: The story supplies several words with visible suffixes — 'friendly', 'suddenly', 'carrying' — so the grammatical concept is grounded directly in text students have already read. Students frequently confuse the suffix -ed (past tense marker) with -ed as a derivational suffix; use 'called' and 'showed' from the table to clarify. Spelling changes in words like 'carrying' (carry → carrying) are worth pausing on briefly because they recur across many common words.

periods.activity_title: Adjectives in Action: Describing Mario and Matching Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.66): write adjectives around Mario's image to describe his character.
Let us learn (p.67): match adjectives to nouns and write adjective-noun phrases and sentences.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.67): complete the paragraph using adjective-noun pairings from the word box.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the line from the story 'Mario, brave and determined, took the strange invisible chair…' (p.66). Ask students what kind of words 'brave' and 'determined' are and what work they do in the sentence, building toward the definition of adjectives.

Students write adjectives around the image of Mario on p.66, drawing on words from the story and their own vocabulary. Share and discuss: which adjectives from the story, and which are students' own additions?

Students complete the adjective-noun matching table at p.67 (brave, clever, tasty, heavy, slight, true × friends, rain, soldier, plan, peanuts, cold), forming phrases in Column C and writing full sentences in Column D.

Pairs share one adjective-noun sentence each. Brief consolidation: the teacher names an adjective from Column A and invites students to volunteer a noun not listed — extending the concept beyond the table.

periods.teacher_notes: Having described the invisible chair's qualities in earlier reading, students are now asked to apply the same descriptive lens to Mario's character; this continuity of method makes the grammar feel purposive rather than abstract. A common pitfall is students selecting any adjective for any noun without considering meaning; the sentence-writing step in Column D forces them to test whether the pairing makes sense. The paragraph-completion task at p.67 is well-suited to independent work at home and does not require prior class preparation.

periods.activity_title: An Acrostic for FRIENDS and Stories Across Cultures

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.70): write an acrostic poem using the letters of FRIENDS.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.70): find a friendship story from your state or another region to share.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the acrostic poem form by writing FRIENDS vertically on the board and modelling one line — for example, 'F — Forever there in the hardest times.' Explain that each line should describe a quality or image of friendship, not just any word starting with that letter.

Students compose their own FRIENDS acrostic poem independently, drawing on qualities, characters, and moments from the story as well as personal ideas. Circulate and encourage vivid, specific lines rather than single adjectives.
Volunteer students read their acrostic poems aloud. Peers listen for the most memorable or unexpected line in each poem and share a brief appreciative response.

Close with a brief note on the homework: students are invited to find a friendship story from their own state or another culture — something from family, community, or memory — which they can share in a future gathering.

periods.teacher_notes: The acrostic form gives students a structural scaffold that keeps the creative task manageable while still requiring original, considered language. Students who default to single adjectives per line should be gently pushed toward phrases or images — for example, 'N — Never leaves when things go wrong' is richer than 'N — Nice'. The homework task of finding a friendship story from a familiar cultural context is exploratory and open; it does not require any resources beyond memory and family conversation.

periods.activity_title: The Invisible Test: A Whole-Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Open synthesis discussion: ask students to explain, in their own words, why grandfather's invisible chair was a better test of friendship than asking someone directly 'Are you my real friend?' This draws on the narrative's central conceit and the listening story of Monika's support.

Vocabulary and language reflection: students recall root words and adjectives from the story (friendly, brave, determined, caring, loyal) and suggest how adding a different suffix or pairing each with a new noun changes the meaning. A quick oral round-table collects examples on the board.

Students write a short paragraph — begun and completed within this unit — contrasting two types of friends: those who stayed to mock Mario and those who silently supported him. Encourage use of adjectives and formed words from the vocabulary work.

Beyond-text comparison: students share what friendship means across the cultures and age groups explored in the chapter — connecting the fable's moral, the listening account, the acrostic form, and any friendship stories from different regions. Close with a shared statement: what, across all these threads, is the one quality every friendship needs?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the narrative's fable-logic, the vocabulary of friendship, the grammar of description, and the broader cultural conversation the beyond-text tasks opened. The short contrast paragraph begins and ends within these forty minutes; no prior draft or piece of writing is continued here. Students from classes that reached this chapter through different routes all share the same story content — the invisible chair, Mario's three true friends, grandfather's lesson — and the synthesis is designed to work from that shared narrative ground alone.
materials: Textbook p.59–70 (any section students wish to consult)

items.item_stem:
Read the statements below about the story 'The Chair' and mark each as True or False.
1. Mario's grandfather challenged him with a wager of fruit chaat to test whether his many companions were truly real friends.
2. Mario successfully sat on the invisible chair on his very first attempt at school.
3. Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently moved behind Mario and held him up so he would not fall.
4. The rest of Mario's classmates helped him repeatedly when he fell from the chair.

options.text: Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently moved behind Mario and held him up so he would not fall.
Mario successfully sat on the invisible chair on his very first attempt at school.
Mario's grandfather challenged him with a wager of fruit chaat to test whether his many companions were truly real friends.
The rest of Mario's classmates helped him repeatedly when he fell from the chair.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — the grandfather explicitly offers fruit chaat as the prize of his wager about Mario's real friends. 2. False — Mario fell repeatedly before finally sitting successfully when his three friends held him up. 3. True — the story describes Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently moving to support Mario. 4. False — the rest of the class did nothing but mock his falls.

items.item_stem: In 'The Chair', grandfather does not simply tell Mario that most of his friends are companions rather than true friends — he devises the invisible-chair test instead. Why do you think grandfather chose this indirect method? What does his choice reveal about how he believed Mario needed to learn this lesson? Support your answer with details from the story.

expected_elements: Grandfather believed Mario needed personal experience, not just words.
The test let Mario discover the truth himself through a real situation.
Reference to the story: Mario's falls while classmates laughed, yet three friends acted.
Insight that indirect lessons can be more powerful than direct advice.

3. Monika is the kind of friend who is always ___________ for you.
4. Manu and Monika have been together through both difficult and ___________ times.

items.item_stem: Manu says in the passage (p.73) that Monika's help and support 'turned into a really good friendship.' In one or two sentences, explain what this phrase means in the context of the passage. What does it suggest about how friendships can develop?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Manu means that what began as practical help — introductions to others, sharing notes — grew into a lasting friendship built on care and shared experience. This suggests that genuine friendship can grow out of small, consistent acts of support rather than starting as an immediate bond.

items.item_stem: In the story 'The Chair', the moment Guneet, Asma, and Deepa silently helped Mario shows that actions can speak louder than words in a friendship. items.item_stem: Think of a person who has been a true friend to you — someone who helped you, stood by you, or made you feel supported. Write a personal message to that friend in your own words. Expresses the writer's personal feeling in response to that action.
Explains in the writer's own voice what the friendship means.

items.item_stem: The narrator of 'The Chair' describes Mario as 'brave and determined' when he carries the invisible chair to school. Choose the adjective from the pair given for each blank and write a sentence of your own using that adjective with a suitable noun from the story. The adjectives to choose between are: (i) brave / boastful — to describe Mario before the test  (ii) caring / mocking — to describe Guneet, Asma, and Deepa during the test. Write one sentence for each adjective you select.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable answers: (i) 'boastful' fits Mario before the test (he constantly brags about his many friends); a sentence such as 'The boastful boy told everyone he had dozens of friends.' (ii) 'caring' fits Guneet, Asma, and Deepa (they silently moved to hold Mario up); a sentence such as 'The caring friends quietly stood behind Mario so he would not fall again.'

Each line of your poem should describe a quality, image, or moment connected to friendship — drawing on what you know about true friendship from your reading, listening, or personal experience. Your poem should have exactly seven lines, one for each letter, and each line should be a phrase or complete thought, not a single word.

expected_elements: Exactly seven lines, each beginning with the correct letter of FRIENDS.
Each line is a phrase or complete thought, not a single word.
At least three lines connect to a quality or event related to friendship.
Language is expressive and chosen with care, not mechanical.

items.item_stem: The story 'The Chair' comes from one cultural setting, but friendship stories exist in every culture and age group. Find or recall one story about friendship from your own state, another region of India, or another country. Write a short project response (one paragraph of five to seven sentences) that: (a) describes what happens in the friendship story you found or recalled, (b) identifies the one quality of true friendship it celebrates, and (c) explains one similarity or difference between that story and what grandfather teaches Mario in 'The Chair'.

expected_elements: Names a specific friendship story from a region or culture.
Identifies clearly one quality of friendship the chosen story celebrates.
States one meaningful similarity or difference with grandfather's lesson.
Written in five to seven connected sentences with a clear paragraph shape.
